figures.caption: Figure 4: Robustness and certification reliability of GeoCert. (a) Noise robustness. Forecasting accuracy under additive Gaussian noise for varying noise levels (0–20 %). GeoCert (red) maintains the lowest mean squared error (MSE) across all noise intensities, with minimal variance, while transformer-based methods exhibit error amplification proportional to noise magnitude. (b) Temporal stability. Forecast trajectories of normalized electrical load over time of day, highlighting interpretable physical regularity across morning (5–9 h) and evening (16–20 h) peaks. GeoCert aligns closely with ground truth across both regimes, whereas competing models overshoot during peak transitions. (c) Certified robustness. Certification probability ρ versus perturbation bound ε , showing an average +83 % improvement over α-CROWN. GeoCert preserves certification validity up to ε = 0.20, indicating sustained formal robustness under increasing input uncertainty.

GeoCert unifies hyperbolic geometry and spectral–constraint integration, achieving the fastest convergence and highest certification rate among all variants and baselines. Best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 5: Comparison of certified forecasting methods. Both α-CROWN and GeoCert provide formal guarantees, but differ fundamentally in certification paradigm, computational scaling, and integration with forecasting.
Table 6: Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis of GeoCert on the Electricity dataset with forecast length H = 96 and lookback L = 96. Best results are highlighted in bold.

Figure 1: Overview of the GeoCert architecture for certified scientific forecasting. (a) Neural Spectral Processing. Multiscale time series inputs (e.g., energy, weather, traffic) are decomposed using an adaptive neural FFT transform with real-time frequency filter banks and multi-head spectral attention, followed by neural Laplace reconstruction. (b) Deep Constraint Networks. Forecasting occurs on a hyperbolic manifold Hd where feasible regions Mvalid are defined by spectral–geometric constraints; verification arises from geodesic flow on the Poincaré sphere, yielding intrinsic proof objects P for certified validity. (c) Performance Analytics. Empirical ablations show consistent improvement in MSE and MAE relative to baselines (PathST, iTransformer, FEDformer, α-crown), as well as higher training speed, convergence rate, and memory efficiency. (d) Conceptual Summary. GeoCert integrates four synergistic components: spectral neural processing, deep constraint intelligence, hyperbolic geometric learning, and certified intelligence for real-time scientific computing.

Figure 2: Geometric foundations of GEOCERT. The framework integrates spectral analysis with hyperbolic geometry for certified time series forecasting. (a–d) Architectural components: (a) Multi-scale spectral decomposition. (b) Hyperbolic constraint manifold Hd with curvature-encoded hierarchies. (c) Gradient-based constraint optimization. (d) Certified output with formal reliability guarantees.

Table 1: Comprehensive benchmarking of GeoCert and baselines across multivariate forecasting datasets. We present comprehensive results of GeoCert and baselines on the Electricity, Exchange, Weather, Solar-Energy, and PEMS08 datasets. The lookback length L is fixed at 96, and the forecast length T varies across 96, 192, 336, and 720. Bold font denotes the best model and underline denotes the second best. All baseline results referenced from prior implementations (9, 16, 17). Certification rate is reported only for methods that generate formal or intrinsic certificates of validity; for other baselines, certification metrics are not defined.

Table 2: Predictive, feasibility, and certification behavior under physical constraints. Metrics are organized by conceptual category: Predictive performance assesses forecasting accuracy; Feasibility quantifies empirical constraint satisfaction; and Certification evaluates formal guarantees of validity. Certification metrics are reported only for certifying approaches (GeoCert and α-CROWN) (Cert. Time (ms) denotes time for each instance), highlighting differences between heuristic constraint enforcement and verifiable computation.

Figure 3: Comprehensive performance characterization of GeoCert. (a) Prediction efficiency. Improvement from one-epoch to final training, measured by MSE and MAE. Green bars denote absolute gains and percentage labels show rapid convergence efficiency. (b) Scalability. Training time per epoch versus dataset cardinality, demonstrating near-logarithmic growth and comparable scaling to transformer variants. (c) Training efficiency. Convergence achieved in four epochs with low average training cost. (d) Relative speed. GeoCert stands as baseline, achieving 39.6×, 10.4×, 1.4×, and 2.8× speed-ups over PatchTST, αCrown iTransformer, and FEDformer respectively. (e) Cost–accuracy trade-off. Total GPU hours versus performance score (1/MSE). GeoCert attains a 97.5% cost reduction relative to PatchTST while maintaining accuracy near the Pareto frontier. (f) Radar summary. Multi-dimensional comparison across six aspects, training speed, computational efficiency, convergence rate, memory efficiency, final accuracy, and early-stage performance, showing that GeoCert(red) consistently achieves balanced, high-efficiency learning across all dimensions.
